content.text:
The drawing is a fragment with two wavy lines, so it has two attachment points.

The ring is a benzene. Its top-right carbon carries a quaternary carbon, which is bonded to a methyl group (the plain line going right). That carbon has a wavy line crossing the bond on its left side, where it joins the ring. A second wavy line sits on the bond going up and to the right, from the carbon toward the top. The wavy lines are drawn at the bond from the ring carbon to the CH carbon and at the bond from that carbon going down-right. The drawing therefore shows a carbon with three substituents: the aryl ring, a methyl, and one more wavy bond.

In the image, the central carbon at about (335, 68) has:
- a line to the left, to the ring at (285, 65), crossed by a wavy line,
- a line to the right, to the methyl at (385, 45), which is plain,
- a wavy line going down-right to (375, 60).

The wavy bonds are therefore the one crossing the ring-to-carbon bond and the one going down-right. Taking the methyl as plain, the carbon is CH(CH3) with two attachment points, one on the ring side and one on the other wavy bond. Written as the carbon with its ring, methyl and attachment point: *C(C)c1cc(Cl)ccc1F, plus a second * for the other wavy line, which would make the carbon *C(C)(*)... However, the wavy line crossing the ring-to-carbon bond marks the attachment of the ring-bearing carbon to the rest of the molecule, and the other wavy line is the continuation of the same bond type. I read this as a single attachment point on the ring-to-carbon bond, giving a 1-arylethyl group, with a second * on the carbon.

The ring numbering: the carbon bearing the side chain (C1) is adjacent to the carbon bearing F (C2) and, on the other side, to a CH next to the carbon bearing Cl. Cl is at the top-left carbon, which is meta to C1 across the ring, so Cl is at position 5 and F at position 2.

Final SMILES, with two attachment points on the central carbon:

SMILES: *C(*)(C)c1cc(Cl)ccc1F
